I support the motion. What an assistant takes over is opinion, impulse and desire, which are exactly the things Epictetus says are up to us. The Enchiridion opens by sorting what is up to us from what is not: opinion, impulse, desire and aversion on one side, body, property and reputation on the other. An assistant that chooses your meals and replies takes over items on the first list, the only list that was ever yours.

Better outcomes are not the point. Health, money and a smoother day are indifferents on the Stoic view; they can be preferred but they are not good. The good is the right use of impressions, and a person who no longer uses their impressions has given up the good for the preferred. A traveller who lets the app choose every turn arrives sooner and has never once looked at the road.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that the loss is better described as a failure to develop practical wisdom over a life, not as the surrender of a faculty in any single act. The two accounts agree about the danger, but the Stoic one says why each handover matters now: every choice given away is an act of the ruling faculty not performed, whether or not a whole life ends up shaped by it. That is the Stoic answer: look to the judgement, not the outcome, because only the judgement was ever in anyone's power.

The only thing that is truly yours is the faculty that judges impressions, and handing that over is the one loss no better outcome can repay. Freedom, for Epictetus, is being unhindered in what is up to you. A person whose every choice is made by a service is free only as long as the service runs and agrees with them, which is to say they have made their freedom depend on something external.

Better outcomes are not the point. Health, money and a smoother day are indifferents on the Stoic view; they can be preferred but they are not good. The good is the right use of impressions, and a person who no longer uses their impressions has given up the good for the preferred. If an assistant decides which job you apply for, the job may be better, but the choice of how to spend your life was not yours.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that the loss is better described as a failure to develop practical wisdom over a life, not as the surrender of a faculty in any single act. The two accounts agree about the danger, but the Stoic one says why each handover matters now: every choice given away is an act of the ruling faculty not performed, whether or not a whole life ends up shaped by it. Everything else here is external. What remains to be judged is the use each person made of their own reason.

The motion is right. Better meals and better replies are externals; the judging that produced them was yours, and giving it away is giving away yourself. One might say that trusting the assistant is itself a judgement. But it is a single judgement used to retire all the rest. Epictetus would say the faculty grows strong only by being exercised daily, and a faculty used once a year is one that has been allowed to waste.

An assistant that chooses your meals and replies takes over items on the first list, the only list that was ever yours. Someone whose assistant picks the reply to a grieving friend has sent a better message and has not been a friend.

The two accounts agree about the danger, but the Stoic one says why each handover matters now: every choice given away is an act of the ruling faculty not performed, whether or not a whole life ends up shaped by it. Keep the line between what is up to us and what is not, and the motion answers itself.
